stages.name: Contested
stages.desc: Rival fleets fight over the region's harbours

stages.name: Carthaginian
stages.desc: Carthage or its allied Phoenician cities hold the main naval bases

stages.name: Greek
stages.desc: Greek cities and kingdoms hold the main naval bases

stages.name: Roman
stages.desc: Rome holds the main naval bases

states.name: Spain
timeline: Phoenician Gadir and the southern ports, in Carthage's sphere; Greek Emporion in the north-east
Hamilcar Barca lands at Gadir to build a new empire in Iberia
Hasdrubal founds Carthago Nova on a sheltered natural harbour
Roman forces under the Scipios land at Emporion
A Roman fleet defeats the Carthaginian squadron at the mouth of the Ebro
Scipio storms Carthago Nova, Carthage's main base in Spain
Gades, the last Carthaginian city in Spain, goes over to Rome

states.name: Libya
timeline: Greek Cyrene and its port Apollonia; Carthage's trading towns lie west of the Altars of the Philaeni
Cyrenaica passes to Ptolemy of Egypt and his Greek fleet

states.name: Tunisia
timeline: Carthage and its harbours on the Gulf of Tunis, heart of a Phoenician sea empire
Agathocles of Syracuse lands on Cape Bon and burns his own ships
Agathocles' army collapses and he flees back to Sicily
A Roman army under Regulus lands at Aspis and marches on Carthage
Xanthippus defeats Regulus outside Tunis
The Mercenary War: unpaid troops and Libyan rebels besiege Carthage
Hamilcar Barca crushes the revolt
Scipio lands near Utica and carries the war to Africa
Peace: Carthage keeps only ten triremes, yet the round harbour rises within its walls
Rome declares war and lays siege to Carthage
Scipio Aemilianus blocks the harbour mouth; a new fleet breaks out through a secret channel
Carthage is stormed and destroyed; its land becomes the Roman province of Africa

states.name: Greece
timeline: Athens, Corinth and the other Greek naval powers
Corcyra places itself under Roman protection after the First Illyrian War
The Second Macedonian War brings Roman fleets into Greek waters
Rome destroys the Macedonian kingdom at Pydna
Rome sacks Corinth; Greece passes under Roman rule

states.name: Italy
timeline: Syracuse under Dionysius I has the strongest fleet in the west; Carthage holds western Sicily and Sardinia
Dionysius destroys Motya; Carthage strikes back and besieges Syracuse
Peace leaves Syracuse the leading naval power
War with Agathocles: Carthage besieges Syracuse again
Peace with Agathocles; the Greek harbours of the east coast stay Syracusan
Pyrrhus campaigns in Sicily; Rome advances through southern Italy
The First Punic War begins over Messana
After the Aegates battle, Sicily becomes Rome's first province
Syracuse falls to Rome after a two-year siege

states.name: Malta
timeline: Phoenician harbours of Malta and Gozo, under Carthaginian rule
A Roman fleet raids and ravages the islands
The Carthaginian garrison surrenders to the consul Sempronius

events.title: Motya falls
events.text: Dionysius I of Syracuse storms the Phoenician island city of Motya, Carthage's base in western Sicily.

events.title: Lilybaeum founded
events.text: Survivors of Motya resettle on the nearby headland of Lilybaeum, soon Carthage's great fortress-harbour.

events.title: Siege of Syracuse
events.text: Himilco's fleet and army besiege Syracuse until plague breaks the camp and his ships are burned.

events.title: Treaty with Rome
events.text: Carthage and Rome renew a treaty dividing the sea; Romans may not trade or found towns beyond its limits.

events.title: Battle of the Crimisus
events.text: Timoleon of Corinth routs a Carthaginian army in western Sicily.

events.title: Ptolemy takes Cyrene
events.text: The Greek cities of Cyrenaica pass to Ptolemy, ruler of Egypt.

events.title: Agathocles in Africa
events.text: Blockaded in Syracuse, Agathocles slips out, lands on Cape Bon and burns his ships to force his men on.

events.title: Agathocles flees
events.text: His African army defeated, Agathocles escapes to Sicily, abandoning his sons and soldiers.

events.title: Pyrrhus defeated at sea
events.text: A Carthaginian fleet mauls Pyrrhus' ships in the Strait of Messina as he leaves Sicily.

events.title: Tarentum surrenders
events.text: The great Greek harbour city of southern Italy falls to Rome.

events.title: War over Messana
events.text: Rome sends troops to Messana in Sicily, starting the First Punic War.

events.title: Battle of Mylae
events.text: Rome's first great fleet, with its boarding bridges, defeats Carthage off northern Sicily.

events.title: Malta raided
events.text: A Roman fleet ravages Carthage's island of Malta.

events.title: Battle of Ecnomus
events.text: In one of the largest sea battles of antiquity, Rome breaks a Carthaginian fleet off southern Sicily.

events.title: Regulus lands
events.text: A Roman army lands at Aspis on Cape Bon and marches on Carthage.

events.title: Regulus defeated
events.text: The Spartan mercenary Xanthippus leads Carthage to victory outside Tunis; Regulus is captured.

events.title: Battle of Drepana
events.text: Adherbal destroys a Roman fleet, Carthage's greatest naval victory of the war.

events.title: Battle of the Aegates
events.text: Lutatius Catulus sinks the Carthaginian relief fleet; Carthage sues for peace and leaves Sicily.

events.title: Mercenary War
events.text: Unpaid mercenaries and Libyan subjects rise against Carthage in a merciless war.

events.title: Rome seizes Sardinia
events.text: While Carthage is weak, Rome takes Sardinia and demands more tribute.

events.title: Hamilcar in Spain
events.text: Hamilcar Barca lands at Gadir to rebuild Carthage's power in Iberia.

events.title: Carthago Nova
events.text: Hasdrubal founds New Carthage on one of the finest harbours of Spain.

events.title: Siege of Saguntum
events.text: Hannibal takes Saguntum, Rome's ally, after an eight-month siege.

events.title: Malta falls to Rome
events.text: The consul Sempronius takes Malta as Rome's fleets command the sea.

events.title: Battle of the Ebro
events.text: A Roman fleet surprises the Carthaginian squadron at the river mouth.

events.title: Battle of Cannae
events.text: Hannibal, who came by land, annihilates a Roman army in Apulia.

events.title: Syracuse falls
events.text: Rome takes Syracuse after a long siege; Archimedes is killed.

events.title: New Carthage stormed
events.text: Scipio crosses the lagoon at low water and takes Carthago Nova in a day.

events.title: Gades surrenders
events.text: The last Carthaginian stronghold in Spain goes over to Rome.

events.title: Scipio lands in Africa
events.text: Scipio's army lands near Utica and besieges the city.

events.title: Battle of Zama
events.text: Scipio defeats Hannibal; Carthage must accept Rome's terms.

events.title: The fleet burned
events.text: Carthage may keep only ten triremes; Scipio burns hundreds of its ships at sea.

events.title: Cynoscephalae
events.text: Rome defeats Philip V of Macedon and declares the Greeks free.

events.title: Hannibal in office
events.text: As chief magistrate, Hannibal reforms Carthage's finances; within a year he is driven into exile.

events.title: Battle of Pydna
events.text: Rome destroys the Macedonian kingdom.

events.title: The Emporia seized
events.text: The Numidian king Masinissa seizes Carthage's towns on the Lesser Syrtis; Rome refuses to intervene.

events.title: Carthage disarmed
events.text: Carthage hands over its weapons; when ordered to abandon the city, it chooses war.

events.title: Scipio's mole
events.text: Scipio Aemilianus builds a great stone dyke across the harbour mouth.

events.title: The secret fleet
events.text: Through a channel dug in secret, fifty new triremes sail out of the harbour.

events.title: The Cothon stormed
events.text: Laelius' troops seize the round naval harbour in the final assault.

events.title: Carthage destroyed
events.text: After six days of street fighting, the Byrsa falls and the city is burned.

events.title: Corinth sacked
events.text: In the same year Rome sacks Corinth, ending Greek independence.

chartNote: Share of the area of six modern countries (Libya cut off south of 29.5°N), coloured by who held each one's main naval bases. Regions are today's boundaries; ancient coasts were divided, and Italy in particular held Carthaginian, Greek and Roman harbours at once. A simplification: dates are turning points, not sharp switches.
